chapter: State of the country and the anthem
title: National anthem controversies, Marvin Gaye and the origins of the Star Spangled Banner
summary: Rowe notes controversial anthem performances; Jang covers the tune's origins, America the Beautiful, and Francis Scott Key as creative transformer.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I think it’s curious, those controversial performances, the “Star Spangled Banner” and these sports teams or whatever, they hire these people and then they’re so surprised and sometimes angry when the person sings like they do. Like you were expecting Marvin Gaye to sing the national anthem like an opera singer or like someone with great respect. And he sings it like he wants to and everybody gets bent out of shape. And it’s just curious that, well why are you hiring these people then, if you don’t want them to sing like they do.

Yeah. And I mean that was Marvin Gaye who won the coveted Grammy award for “Sexual Healing.” And then the ironic part is that the melody of the “Star Spangled Banner” by John Stafford Smith was an 18th century British sex and drinking song, so actually and ironically Marvin Gaye was actually respecting the tradition of where it came from, which is actually Brit — I mean “America the Beautiful,” actually that was by two composers — the melody was from Samuel Augustus Ward, and then Katharine Lee Bates. And that’s powerful, because it was a woman composer, an American woman composer. And so there was talk about changing the national anthem from the “Star Spangled Banner” to “America the Beautiful.” That was actually 1989 by Senator Andrew Jacobs, who was a democrat from Indiana, and he was a disabled Marine veteran. So what was great about that — not whether he was a democrat or republican — is that he said well we should not abandon the “Star Spangled Banner,” it should be for specific, like military — you know because the military is about sort of you can’t — it’s no nonsense, see that’s the whole culture. You know you have to — any kind of deviation and that’s uncalled for. And it has to be, because you’re at war your whole life. So I understand that. And that’s why I would play it, if I perform it, I would respect that. Because these are people that are fighting for your country. But then if you also want to say think out of the box, and even if you think of the creative process, which was not a collaboration between John Stafford Smith and Francis Scott Key — Francis Scott Key took something and he made something new out of it, right? Because the words was not about Anacreon, it was not about the god of love and pleasure, of wine and women, it was about being captive on the ship and seeing your country being bombed, and then the flag is there. And he’s an amateur lawyer, or amateur poet and he’s a lawyer. But he was inspired to write words to it. So the story about that — and that was something that you could argue was not only inspiring but sort of, you know, he was changing the tradition of the song. So, you know, I think we need to look deeply into the history and deeply — instead of this reaction. So that’s why I don’t think of it as hey, these are the republicans © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-

that are over there, these are the democrats that are over there, these are the Marines. I think in some ways Barack Obama tried to bring the country together. I mean he had Aretha Franklin sing “My Country ‘Tis of Thee,” which is actually only like six pitches in range, vocal range, an easy song to sing. And this time he had what, like Kelly Clarkson, you know? So I mean he had a multi-cultural — he had classical music and art — Aaron Copland. He had “Simple Gifts” the time before. So he’s — I mean that’s what impressed me was his inauguration. The artists that need to be included, not just the celebrities, but we’re all together. And I also, yeah, I mean Beyonce and Jay-Z, I know that they were criticized by Harry Belafonte who is somebody that I greatly respect. But they cannot be, you know, they’re black artists but they have a role that they can contribute. I think as I grow older I’m trying to not expect the younger generation to follow what I’ve done or even my predecessors. It’s just like — well my daughter for example, is 18 years old. She has to find her journey. And hopefully the value of integrity and being honest and doing what’s real is most important.
